title: Monotonic stack: largest rectangle
summary: Largest rectangle under a histogram. Keep bar indices with rising heights; a shorter bar pops each taller one and measures how far it spans. A trailing 0 flushes the stack. O(n).
code: # Heights rise up the stack; a shorter bar closes every taller one.
width = index if not stack else index - stack[-1] - 1
triggers: for each bar, how far it extends left and right before something shorter
largest area or score limited by the smallest value in a range
prompts: A street of equal-width buildings is given as their heights. What is the largest rectangular banner that fits entirely within the buildings' outline?
Books of equal thickness but different heights stand side by side. What is the largest rectangular label you could stick across their spines without any of it rising above a book?
invariant: Heights at the stack's indices rise from bottom to top, and a popped bar spans from just after the bar below it to just before index.
mantra: A shorter bar pops and measures every taller one.
pitfalls: After a pop, width is index - stack[-1] - 1, or index when the stack is empty.
Append a sentinel 0 so every bar is popped and measured at the end.
Store indices: the width comes from positions, the height from heights[index].

anchors.name: Maximal Rectangle
anchors.trick: Build each row's histogram of consecutive 1s above it, then run this per row.

anchors.name: Sum of Subarray Minimums
anchors.trick: The same pops count how many subarrays each value is the minimum of.

anchors.name: Trapping Rain Water
anchors.trick: Decreasing stack instead: a taller bar pops and fills the dip between it and the new top.

mutations.replacement: width = index if not stack else index - stack[-1]
mutations.explanation: Counts the shorter bar below as part of the span, so every width after a pop is one too wide.
Without the trailing 0, bars still on the stack are never measured: [1, 2, 3] gives 0 instead of 4.
